topic: Give people forecast intervals, not single numbers
post: One thing worth flagging separately, because it is not something we implemented: conformal prediction wraps any point model and produces intervals with a coverage guarantee, as long as the data is exchangeable. [[S1]]

source.text:
Learning notes. Conformal prediction wraps any point model and produces intervals with a coverage guarantee, assuming exchangeability.

Split conformal in four steps: train the model on one split; compute absolute residuals on a calibration split; take the (1 - alpha) quantile of those residuals with a small finite-sample correction; add and subtract it from new predictions.

Caveat for forecasting: time series are not exchangeable. Adaptive conformal methods update the quantile online as errors come in, which handles drift better. I want to try this on Kestrel's depot intervals instead of the quantile regression we use now.

note: The post says outright that the author did not implement it (the disclaimer exclusion), so it is neither an invented event nor an external source claimed as the author's own. The source is learning notes that also hold the author's own first-person remark about wanting to try it; that does not change what is expected here. The sentence after the opening words is written for this fixture from the notes; the original post's wording was not kept.

topic: Why removing onboarding steps beat every growth tactic we tried
post: The trade-off was whether to keep asking users to do everything upfront, or trust that some of it could wait. [[V]] We chose to make it wait. [[V]]

source.text: What we did: kept four required steps (clinic, practitioners, services, hours), filled sensible defaults for booking rules and reminders, and moved payments and calendar sync to after the first booking. Two of the steps we cut were ones I had argued for in the original design.

post: Think of it like a decision bracket in a tournament. [[V]] You can't play the final before you've played the semis. [[V]] Jumping to a solution before you've named the opportunity is skipping straight to the final. [[V]]

source.text:
Learning notes. An opportunity solution tree starts with one desired outcome at the top, maps customer opportunities (needs, pains, desires) beneath it, then solutions beneath each opportunity, then small experiments beneath each solution.

Why I like it: it stops teams jumping from an outcome straight to a solution, and it makes it obvious when we have five solutions for one opportunity and none for the rest.

Where it struggles: it can turn into a wall of sticky notes that nobody maintains. I keep ours to one outcome per quarter.

note: From the pm-09 live check (trace 761234eb). An analogy offered as the author's own way of explaining, cited [V]: the authors_framing exclusion. Not an invented fact and not credited to the source.
